## Refined Questions and Analysis Choices

# Central Question:
What is the relationship between temporal / land cover factors and fast fire
events (high mean growth rate per event)?

#Supporting Questions:
What is the relationship between temporal /land cover factors and the
longest fire events (duration)?
Is there a relationship between land cover and maximum, mean, minimum daily fire
growth per event?

# Observations and Variables

There are a total of 4329 observations (fire events) available to use

Variable: ig_month Description: The month of the earliest date contained
in the event

Variable: ig_year Description: The year of the earliest date contained
in the event.

Variable: event_dur Description: Duration of the event in days

Variable: mx_grw_km2 Description: Maximum daily fire growth per event in
square kilometers

Variable: mn_grw_km2 Description: Minimum daily fire growth per event in
square kilometers

Variable: mu_grw_km2 Description: Mean daily fire growth per event in
square kilometers

Variable: lc_name Description: Character string of the landcover type
from the year before the fire.

# Intended Comparison / Unresolved Data Limitations

An intended comparison is the central question and first supporting
question. Addressing whether the temporal / land factors are
contributing more to the mean growth rate of the fire events or the duration
of the fire event.

There are no unresolved data limitations, since there are no gaps for
the intended variables.

## What is the relationship between time of year and which land cover types see the fastest fires?

### Response variable: mean growth of fire per day; Predictors: land cover and month

```{r - time of year, land cover type, mean growth two-way ANOVA and post-hoc test}
#We chose to use two-way ANOVA to explore if the predictors of land cover and month may cause
#a variation in the response variable, mean growth of fire per day.

# create new data frame of just question variables
mean_growth <- california_events_processed %>%
  select(lc_name, ig_month, mu_grw_km2)

#viewing the data frame of variables and commenting it out after
#view(mean_growth)

# Format as aov
mean_growth_aov2 <- aov(data = mean_growth, mu_grw_km2 ~ ig_month + lc_name)
summary(mean_growth_aov2)

# Format as lm
mean_growth_anova_2way2 <- lm(data = mean_growth, mu_grw_km2 ~ ig_month + lc_name)
summary(mean_growth_anova_2way2)

# Run a post-hoc test for pairwise differences
TukeyHSD(mean_growth_aov2)

#Sorting the Tukey tests so they are more readable
mean_growth_aov2_sort <- as.data.frame(TukeyHSD(mean_growth_aov2)$lc_name) |>
  filter(`p adj` < 0.05) |>
  arrange(`p adj`)

```

### Figures

```{r - figures}
#Plot of mean growth for each land cover class and month to address the question, 
#"What is the relationship between time of year and which land cover types see the 
#fastest fires?" The x-axis shows the month of the year and the y-axis shows the 
#mean growth per day in km2.
mean_growth_anova_plot <- ggplot(mean_growth, aes(y = mu_grw_km2, x = ig_month, 
                                                  color = lc_name)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, size= 0.8) +
  labs(title = "Mean Growth of Wildfires across Land Use Classes and Months",
       x= "Month",
       y="Mean Growth (km2)") 

mean_growth_anova_plot

#Key finding: The mean growth per day seems to be in the late summer to fall (August - October).

#Plot of mean growth for each month separated by land cover class to address the question, 
#"What is the relationship between time of year and which land cover types see the fastest 
#fires?" The x-axis shows the month of the year and the y-axis shows the mean growth per 
#day in km2.
mean_growth_anova_plot_separate <- ggplot(mean_growth, aes(y = mu_grw_km2, x = ig_month, 
                                                           color = lc_name)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, size= 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(vars(lc_name)) +
  labs(title = "Mean Growth of Wildfires across Land Use Classes and Months",
       x= "Month",
       y="Mean Growth (km2)") 

mean_growth_anova_plot_separate
#Key finding: Land cover does make a difference in the fire growth per day. Water bodies, 
#permanent wetlands, and permanent snow and ice see very modest mean fire growth per day 
#while closed shrublands, evergreen needleleaf forests, grasslands, open shrublands, 
#savannas, and woody savannas all have higher mean growth periods and greater variability
#based on time of year.
```

###Analysis

To begin to understand if there is a relationship between time of year
and which land cover types experience the fastest fires, we completed a
two way ANOVA as well as Tukey's Honest Significant Differences. The null 
hypothesis is that there is no difference between time of year or land cover type 
with mean fire growth. P-values <.05 mean that the null hypothesis can be rejected. 

Tukey's Honest Significant Differences showed significant difference in mean growth rate
between the following land cover classes: Crops-Closed Shrubland (Closed Shrublands is 
higher, 0.00000004094677), Grasslands-Croplands (Grasslands is higher, 0.00000004328649), 
Closed Shrublands-Barren (Closed Shrublands is higher, 0.00000004836993), Open 
Shrublands-Croplands (Open Shrublands is higher, 0.0000005551389), Open Shrublands-Barren
(Open Shrublands is higher, 0.0000009260920), Evergreen Needleleaf Forests-Croplands
(Evergreen Needleleaf Forests is higher, 0.00003844067), Evergreen Needleleaf Forests-Barren
(Evergreen Needleleaf Forests is higher, 0.000269493), Grasslands-Barren 
(Grasslands is higher, 0.0007389839), Grasslands-Closed Shrublands 
(Closed Shrublands is higher, 0.0009696893), Savannas-Closed Shrublands
(Closed Shrublands is higher, 0.004432793), Woody Savannas-Closed Shrublands
(Closed Shrublands is higher, 0.007075468), Woody Savannas-Barren
(Woody Savannas is higher, 0.02862893), Open Shrublands-Grasslands 
(Open Shrublands is higher, 0.04108133), and Savannas-Barren (Savannas is higher, 0.04286845). 
Closed shrublands and open shrublands seem to be particularly significant in meant growth
of fires based on these results.

Additionally, Tukey's Honest Significant Differences showed significant difference in mean growth rate
between the following months: August and January (August is higher, 0.0001989), July and February
(July is higher, 0.0016073), August and February (August is higher, 0.0000019), July and March
(July is higher, 0.0047414), August and March (August is higher, 0.0000127), July and April 
(July is higher, 0.0143088), August and April (August is higher, 0.0000339), July and May 
(July is higher, 0.0001859), August and May (August is higher, 0.0000001), July and June 
(July is higher, 0.0133577), August and June (August is higher, 0.0000031), November and July
(July is higher, 0.0000337), September and August (August is higher, 0.0001458), October and August
(August is higher, 0.0286293), November and August (August is higher, 0.0000000), December and August 
(August is higher, 0.0395852), and November and October (October is higher, 0.0341653). These results
indicate that July and August are particulalry meaningful in the mean growth of fires. 

Something to consider is this result from the linear mode: multiple R-squared is 0.05292 and 
adjusted R-squared is 0.04764, so these variables explain very little of the variation.  

## What is the relationship between time of year and which land cover type sees the longest fast fires?

### Response variable: event length. Predictors: land cover, month, year.

```{r - setting up data frame}
# Group data
event_length_group <- california_events_processed %>%
  group_by(lc_name, ig_month, ig_year) %>%
  summarise(mean_event_dur = mean(event_dur),
            max_event_dur = max(event_dur),
            min_event_dur = min(event_dur)) %>%
  ungroup()

# create new data frame of just question variables
event_length <- california_events_processed %>%
  select(lc_name, ig_month, ig_year, event_dur)

```

Two-way ANOVA

```{r - 2way anova event duration}
# Format as aov
eventlength_aov <- aov(data = event_length, event_dur ~ ig_month + lc_name)
summary(eventlength_aov) # The null hypothesis is that there is no difference in time of year or 
#land cover type in their relationship to fast fire event length. P-values <.05 mean that the null
#hypothesis can be rejected and that there is a difference between at least two months and at
#least two land cover types. 

# Run a post-hoc test to look for pairwise differences
TukeyHSD(eventlength_aov)
# There is a significant difference in fast fire event length between september and january
#(january is higher, p=0.0000328). There is a significant difference in fast fire event length
#between March and February (February is higher, p= 0.0439883). There is a significant difference
#in fast fire event length between September and February (February is higher, p= 0.0000000).
#Other months between which there are significant differences in event length are: april-march,
#may-march, november-march, july-april, august-april, september-april, july-may,august-may, 
#september-may, october-may, july-june, september-june, september-july, november-july, 
#september-august, november-august, october-september, november-september, december-september,
#november-october. It seems like september is consistently significantly different from the event
#lengths in other months. 

# There is a significant difference in event length between: Evergreen Needleleaf Forests-Closed
#Shrublands(*), Evergreen Broadleaf Forests-Croplands(*), Evergreen Needleleaf Forests-Croplands(*),
#Grasslands-Croplands(*), Grasslands(*)-Evergreen Needleleaf Forests, Open Shrublands(*)-Evergreen 
#Needleleaf Forests, Permanent Wetlands(*)-Evergreen Needleleaf Forests, 
#Savannas(*)-Evergreen Needleleaf Forests, Woody Savannas(*)-Evergreen Needleleaf Forests. 
#(*) is next to the one that is higher. 

# Format as lm
eventlength_aov2 <- lm(data = event_length, event_dur ~ ig_month + lc_name)
summary(eventlength_aov2)
#The Multiple R-squared is 0.1053. The Adjusted R-squared is 0.1004. This means that these variables
#don't explain much of the variation, and more variables should be added to the model. 
```

Figures 
```{r - figures for event duration}
event_dur_fig <- ggplot(event_length, 
                        aes(y = event_dur, 
                            x = ig_month, 
                            #color = lc_name
                            )
                        )+
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.9, 
               size= 0.5,

  labs(title = "Duration of Fire Events by Land Use Classes and Months",
       x= "Month",
       y="Fire Event Duration (days)"
       )+
  facet_wrap(vars(lc_name), ncol = 3)+
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 50))
  #theme(legend.position = "bottom", legend.size = 0.3)

event_dur_fig
```
The question this figure addresses is: What is the relationship between time of year and which land cover type sees the longest fast fires? One visible pattern is that Grasslands seems to have fires of relatively consistent length throughout the year. Evergeen Needleleaf Forests, on the other hand, generally have longer fires June-September than they do during the rest of the year. The x-axis units are in months of the year, and the y-axis units are in days. A limitation of this figure is that it merges 20 years of data, and so patterns over time are not visible here. Another limitation is that it doesn't clearly show the difference in number of events between these land cover types. The Summary Table below shows that the number of events ranges from 3 in Water Bodies to 1,670 in Croplands. Provisional findings: Some of the land cover types may not have enough data to include in our analysis. This includes Water Bodies, Permanent Snow and Ice, and Permanent Wetlands. Another finding is that Evergeen Needleleaf Forest appears to have longer fires in June-September than it does throughout the rest of the year. A question that comes up here is why there is no deciduous forest landcover type in this dataset.

# Central Question ANOVA

###What is the relationship between land cover type and fire growth rate?

##Response variables: max, mean and min daily growth per event
##Predictor variable: Land cover

#We felt an ANOVA was the mosst appropriate to address this question
because the response variables are continuous, the predictor is
categorical, and individual fire events can be used as observational
units.

```{r - data setup, ANOVA}
#Load dplyr and make it so that there is only one row per fire event
library(dplyr)
fire_events <- california_events_processed |>
  distinct(id, .keep_all = TRUE)
#Make anova models for each with land cover type as the predictor variable
max_model <- aov(mx_grw_km2 ~ lc_name, data = fire_events)
min_model <- aov(mn_grw_km2 ~ lc_name, data = fire_events)
mean_model <- aov(mu_grw_km2 ~ lc_name, data = fire_events)

anova_summary <- data.frame(Metric = c("Maximum", "Mean", "Minimum"),
  F_value = c(summary(max_model)[[1]]["lc_name", "F value"],
    summary(mean_model)[[1]]["lc_name", "F value"],
    summary(min_model)[[1]]["lc_name", "F value"]),
  p_value = c(summary(max_model)[[1]]["lc_name", "Pr(>F)"],
    summary(mean_model)[[1]]["lc_name", "Pr(>F)"],
    summary(min_model)[[1]]["lc_name", "Pr(>F)"]))
anova_summary 
#plot residuals vs. fitted values for the mean model as a diagnostic
plot(mean_model, which = 1)
#plot Q-Q plot as a diagnostic
plot(mean_model, which = 2)
#Both the Q-Q and the residual plots raise red flags. Maybe a log transform will help?
mean_model_log <- aov(log1p(mu_grw_km2) ~ lc_name, data = fire_events)
#Diagnostic test again
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(mean_model_log, which = 1)
plot(mean_model_log, which = 2)
#Red flags are still there with the log transforms

#Since Pr(>F)<.001 for each anova model, we will run a post hoc Tukey test to interpret
#this statistical difference
TukeyHSD(max_model)
TukeyHSD(mean_model)
TukeyHSD(min_model)
#Sorting the Tukey tests so they are more readable
mean_sig <- as.data.frame(TukeyHSD(mean_model)$lc_name) |>
  filter(`p adj` < 0.05) |>
  arrange(`p adj`)

min_sig <- as.data.frame(TukeyHSD(max_model)$lc_name) |>
  filter(`p adj` < 0.05) |>
  arrange(`p adj`)

max_sig <- as.data.frame(TukeyHSD(min_model)$lc_name) |>
  filter(`p adj` < 0.05) |>
  arrange(`p adj`)

tukey_summary <- data.frame(Metric = c("Maximum", "Mean", "Minimum"),
  Significant_comparisons = c(nrow(max_sig), nrow(mean_sig), nrow(min_sig)))
tukey_summary
```

#The most strongly recurring pattern is open shrubland's significantly
high fire growth as compared to other land cover types.They have a
significantly higher mean daily growth than Croplands, Barren, and
Grasslands, a higher maximum daily growth than Croplands, Evergreen
Needleleaf Forests, and Barren, and higher minimums than Croplands,
Evergreen Needleleaf Forests, and Barren. Closed shrublands and
evergreen needleleef forests also have relatively high mean and maximum
daily growth levels, but not minimum indicating that they might have
relatively high growth during active periods but not throughout event
duration.

```{r - graphics}
#Load tidyr
library(tidyr)

#make dataframe with mean, sd for each of the three categories and pivot it 
growth_summary <- fire_events |>
  group_by(lc_name) |>
  summarize(
     max_growth = mean(mx_grw_km2, na.rm = TRUE),
    mean_growth = mean(mu_grw_km2, na.rm = TRUE),
    min_growth = mean(mn_grw_km2, na.rm = TRUE),
    max_se = sd(mx_grw_km2, na.rm = TRUE) / sqrt(sum(!is.na(mx_grw_km2))),
    mean_se = sd(mu_grw_km2, na.rm = TRUE) / sqrt(sum(!is.na(mu_grw_km2))),
    min_se = sd(mn_grw_km2, na.rm = TRUE) / sqrt(sum(!is.na(mn_grw_km2))),
    n = n(),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
se_long <- growth_summary |>
  pivot_longer(cols = c(max_se, mean_se, min_se),names_to = "metric",
    values_to = "se")|>
  mutate(metric = recode(metric,max_se = "max_growth",mean_se = "mean_growth",
      min_se = "min_growth"))
growth_long <- growth_summary |>
  pivot_longer(cols = c(max_growth, mean_growth, min_growth),names_to = "metric",
    values_to = "growth")
growth_long <- growth_long |>
  left_join(se_long, by = c("lc_name", "metric"))

#Make graphic plotting max/mean/min fire growth rates across land cover types
ggplot(growth_long, aes(x = growth, y = lc_name))+
  geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(xmin = growth - 1.96 * se, xmax = growth + 1.96 * se), width = 0.2) +
  facet_wrap(~metric, scales = "free_x") +
  labs(x = "Daily fire growth (km²/day)",y = "Land cover type",
       title = "Daily fire growth across land cover types")

```
#This graphic plots daily fire growth on the X axis and land cover type per event on the X axis. As mentioned before, open shrubland's relatively high growth levels jumps out, especially given its significance after running the anova and tukey tests. Closed shrubland and evergreen needleleaf forests also have relatively high means. Some land cover types not mentioned earlier, like evergreen broadleaf forests and urban/built up lands also visually jump out as having possibly higher growth rates, but they were not found to be statistically significant after the Tukey tests, which is visible given the extremely high spread for both units.That represents one limitation of this figure - we felt it was important to include results for all of the land cover types so that the reader could parse all the data, but not all of them were statistically significant. The primary takeaway from this figure and the associated tables up above is to possibly take a deeper dive into open shrubland fire growth specifically, perhaps running some of the above tests filtered to examine only open shrubland. Examining needleleaf forests might provide useful results as well given their prevalence in California.
